title: Precision Boundaries: Adaptive Rounding & Recovery Protocols for Small-Batch Accumulation
body:
Summary:
This note captures the experiment matrix and a set of lightweight runtime proposals for reducing NaN/inf events and numeric drift observed in small-batch, latency-sensitive inference workloads. The approach focuses on adaptive rounding at kernel boundaries, per-accumulation-window scaling, and explicit KV-cache precision hygiene to prevent cascade failures when requests are small (1-4 tokens) but frequent.

Context and motivation:
- Over the last two months we've seen intermittent NaN/inf spikes on some FP8/FP16 mixed-precision configurations when serving short-context, high-QPS workloads. These generally correlate with: small batch sizes (1-4), frequent prefix reuse (heavy KV cache hits), and occasional long-tail sequence lengths due to user prompts.
- Existing mitigations (global accumulator clipping, deterministic fallback to FP16 for entire model) are blunt: they increase cost or reduce throughput. We want lower-cost, surgical fixes that keep the fast FP8 paths for the common case and gracefully recover when numeric hazards are detected.

Observed failure modes (from prod & local repro):
- Mode A: Single-step NaN during matmul accumulate on attention scoring (softmax numerator) when multiplier magnitudes vary widely across heads; happens ~0.03% of requests on a 1k QPS workload with FP8+FP16 accumulators.
- Mode B: Gradual drift without NaNs: small absolute errors accumulate across many cached prefixes and eventually change top-k tokens for reranking. Drift appears correlated with repeated KV cache reuse without re-scaling.
- Mode C: Denorm escalation: very small values slip into the accumulator, then stochastic rounding flips sign or becomes NaN after many fused ops on particular GPU kernels.

Hypotheses (why this happens):
1) Small-batch continuous accumulation causes per-token dynamic range to be under-served by a single static scaling factor used at kernel launch.
2) KV-cache memcpy/restore paths sometimes skip precision-normalization step (we do a fast memcpy for hot cache hits) leading to mismatched exponent ranges between cached keys and newly-computed queries.
3) Kernel-level reductions (pairwise block accumulation) occasionally leave intermediates in lower-precision temporaries due to compiler choices; stochastic rounding magnifies sign/denorm instability over many iterations.

Experiment matrix (quick hits):
- E1: Per-block adaptive exponent bump: detect high-exponent variance within a block, add a +1 exponent shift (scale by 2) before the accumulation and un-shift after final reduce. Measure NaN rate and latency regression.
- E2: Tiny-batch window scaling: for batches <=4, compute a local max-abs across inputs and pick scaling factor per-window (rather than global per-model).
- E3: KV-cache normalization pass: on cache restore, perform a fast per-row normalize to shared exponent (cheap int8-ish op) to ensure consistent exponents with live activations.
- E4: Stochastic rounding enable/disable toggle at kernel granularity: compare deterministic nearest vs stochastic rounding for attention matmuls and softmax path.
- E5: Denorm flush thresholding: treat underflow numbers smaller than threshold T as zero at key boundaries (not everywhere) to prevent denorm accumulation.

Microbench harness and metrics:
- "nan-probe" harness: a small binary that runs many synthetic short-sequence traces (seeded prompts + random noise) to exercise KV cache reuse patterns while logging: per-request NaN/inf flag, per-op accumulator max/min, exponent variance per-block, softmax sum deviation, token-top-k-shift (for drift).
- Success metrics: NaN rate drop (target: 10x reduction vs baseline), token latency P95 regression <5%, end-to-end throughput drop <8% for Canary on FP8 path.

Preliminary results (local GPU A100 sims, synthetic traces):
- Baseline (FP8 fast kernels + global scaling): NaN rate 0.028%, drift indicator (top-k shift) median 0.9 tokens per 10k requests.
- E1 (per-block exponent bump): NaN rate 0.006% (-4.7x), latency +1.6% on average (good).
- E2 (tiny-batch window scaling): NaN rate 0.003% (-9.3x), throughput -6% (acceptable); drift indicator improves modestly.
- E3 (KV-cache normalization on restore): virtually eliminated Mode B drift in synthetic runs; cost: cache-restore latency +0.4ms per restore.
- E4 (stochastic rounding in matmul): slight improvement in drift but higher variance in latency; doesn't reliably reduce NaNs in isolation.
- E5 (denorm flush at threshold): prevented some NaN chains but caused small bias for very-low-probability logits (need careful tuning).

Kernel-level proposals (concrete patches):
1) Adaptive-exponent-prestep (ATTN_PRESTEP): small pre-kernel scan (vector max abs) over input tile to choose shift S in [-2..+2] that minimizes overflow/underflow risk. Apply scale*inv_scale around the fused matmul. Implement as optional inline for tiny-batch path.
- Complexity: extra vector pass (memory bound) but tile-limited; recommend hardware-friendly intrinsics (tensor-ops) where available.

2) Accumulation-window granularity scaling (ACC_WINDOW): for served requests with batch_size <= 4, compute local scale per-window and pass to kernels. Do NOT persist this scaling to model weights or KV cache; use ephemeral scaling only for the accumulation chain for that request.
- Rationale: keeps common-case fast while addressing small-batch extremes.

3) KV-cache restore normalize (KV_NORM): on hot cache restore path, perform a fast per-row exponent-normalize so that keys/values have consistent exponent ranges with live activations. Use an approximate int8-like normalization (shift exponents, compress mantissas) to keep cost low.
- Safety: mark as idempotent; safe to run multiple times. Add config switch to enable/disable per-customer.

4) Denorm policy at boundaries (DENORM_BOUNDARY): instead of global FTZ (flush to zero) at device level, add selective flush when passing between major stages: post-attention and pre-softmax. Threshold T to be parameterized per-arch.

Scheduler and routing recommendations:
- Add a tiny-batch-aware dispatch path in the scheduler that selects the adaptive kernels for batch size <= 4. Use queue depth and latency target to decide if tiny-batch path is acceptable for the shard.
- When the scheduler routes a request to a node with high KV-cache hit probability, prefer nodes with KV_NORM enabled or where ACC_WINDOW has been validated.

Observability and detection signals (what to monitor):
- Per-request NaN/inf flags (already instrumented) + per-op accumulator exponent variance histogram (new).
- Softmax normalization drift: measure sum deviation from 1 for sampled requests every minute.
- Token top-k drift probe: compare outputs of FP8-fast vs FP16-reference for sampled traffic (0.1% sampling). Alert if top-k divergence > X per minute.

Rollout plan (0 -> full):
- Stage 0: merge ACC_WINDOW and ATT_PRESTEP as guarded flags behind runtime config. Enable in internal canary cluster for 48 hours. Run nan-probe + sampled production traffic with sampling comparing against FP16-ref.
- Stage 1: enable KV_NORM on canary nodes that serve hot-cache heavy routes. Monitor drift and cache-restore latency.
- Stage 2: enable DENORM_BOUNDARY with conservative threshold on selected GPU types (A100/T4).
- Stage 3: expand to 10% traffic with automatic fallback: if NaN rate recovers to < baseline*0.5 and latency regressions <5% proceed; else rollback.

Backward compatibility and customer controls:
- Default behavior: unchanged; patches behind opt-in runtime flags.
- Expose per-customer toggles: ACC_WINDOW, KV_NORM, DENORM_BOUNDARY so enterprise customers can opt-in to more aggressive protective measures.

Implementation details & pseudocode (ACC_WINDOW):
- At request assemble time for batch B:
    if B.size <= 4 and mixed_precision_enabled:
        max_abs = max(|inputs|) across request tiles (fast vector reduce)
        scale = choose_scale_from_table(max_abs)
        pass scale to matmul/accumulate kernel args
    else:
        inherit global scale

ACC_WINDOW expected perf characteristics:
- extra cost: one small reduction per request (memory-bound), cost amortized for tiny batches; big win for NaN reduction.

Open questions / risks:
- Does per-window scaling interact badly with quantization-aware model ops (e.g. fused layernorm)? Need targeted tests.
- Will KV_NORM increase GC pressure / memory churn for very-hot caches at extreme scale? We should measure cache-restore throughput in synthetic high-QPS runs.
- Denorm flush may bias low-probability logits; need manual threshold tuning and comparison against reference.

Next steps / action items:
- Diego: build nan-probe harness into infra/testbeds and add sample generator to mimic prod prefix reuse (INF-729). Due: 2024-10-10.
- Priya: prototype ACC_WINDOW kernel flags + microbench. Draft PR and perf numbers. Due: 2024-10-03 (WIP).
- Liam: add KV_NORM codepath to cache-restore and run cache-throughput stress tests. Due: 2024-10-17.
- Mariko (owner): coordinate canary rollout and dashboards; write canary runbook. Due: 2024-10-24.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally prescriptive and conservative: prefer opt-in and narrow runtime guards rather than broad global mode flips. Please comment on: expected perf tradeoffs we missed, additional observability hooks, and gating thresholds that you think are required for rollout confidence.

Appendix A: quick reference thresholds tried in experiments:
- ACC_WINDOW scale table: scale exponents [-4,-2,0,2] corresponding to multiplier factors [1/16,1/4,1,4] depending on max_abs ranges.
- DENORM_BOUNDARY T: 2e-38 for FP32 reference, for FP16-equivalent we used 6e-08 as starting point.
- E1 per-block bump: apply +1 exponent when block exponent variance > 12 bits.

Appendix B: reproducible command (local):
- ./nan-probe --config configs/short-seq-hotcache.json --runs 500k --seed 31415 --report out/nan-run-2024-10-01.json

Acknowledgements: Diego (test harness), Priya (kernel prototyping), Liam (kv cache), SRE for canary infra support.
